channel.title: Midia Reshadi — GPU kernel performance, measured
channel.description: Independent GPU kernel research. Benchmarks and low-level analysis on NVIDIA and AMD hardware, including the experiments that reject my own hypotheses.

item.title: FP8 on Ada with cuda-oxide, checked on real silicon
item.description: cuda-oxide lets you write GPU kernels in Rust. Its FP8 support for Ada (sm_89) was largely auto-generated, so I checked it on a real L4: FP8 conversions and the full m16n8k16 tensor-core MMA family, verified numerically correct against CPU references, with clean PTX. Generated is not the same as verified, so this fills in that gap. 1 figure.

item.title: A cliff below the cache: why a softmax slows down before it should
item.description: A follow-up to the softmax study. On the L4, the bandwidth cliff arrives at ~27 MB, below the 48 MB cache. Why? I guessed multi-pass reuse and was wrong: re-reading one small row costs almost no extra time (confirmed in the PTX). The real cause is that input and output share the cache, so a read-only kernel cliffs at ~55 MB, almost exactly double. 2 figures.

item.title: How close to peak is a simple softmax? Two GPUs, one measurement trap
item.description: Softmax is memory-bound, so the question is simple: what fraction of bandwidth does it reach? I tested three optimizations on an L4 and an MI300X; the data rejected all three. The reason was more interesting than a speedup — most of my measurements were reading cache, not memory, and one GPU showed a mirage the other could not. On measuring your real ceiling, spotting cache-resident benchmarks, and knowing when an operation simply cannot fill the GPU. 3 figures.

item.title: Benchmarking a moving target: my cuda-oxide results changed in weeks
item.description: A follow-up to my cuda-oxide study. Re-testing weeks later, two of three findings had changed — and one change dropped a safe-indexing bounds check, so safe Rust code reads out of bounds (confirmed by compute-sanitizer, reported as cuda-oxide #396). Also: why the version tag does not pin the compiler. 3 figures.

item.title: Found it: the Rust GPU speed gap was a 64-bit loop counter
item.description: Follow-up to the 2×2 study, which left a ~3–5% Rust deficit on the reduction kernel as "cause not established". Reading the SASS pointed at 64-bit (usize) loop indexing; a three-line u32 change removes the gap completely. 3 figures.

item.title: Language or backend? Adding rust-cuda to my GPU code comparison
item.description: A 2×2 follow-up that adds rust-cuda (Rust → libNVVM) to the cuda-oxide study, so language and backend can be separated. The two Rust compilers turn out to make opposite safety choices; the compute-bound speed gap is real but not a pure backend effect. 3 figures.

item.title: Safe Rust on the GPU, at the PTX level: what cuda-oxide actually emits
item.description: A PTX/SASS-level comparison of cuda-oxide (safe Rust to PTX) against clang and nvcc on three GPU kernels — where the overhead comes from, whether it amortizes, and what it costs at runtime on an L4. 3 figures.

item.title: Attention kernels on MI300X: a utilization story
item.description: Benchmarking FlashAttention kernels on AMD MI300X — AITER vs Triton vs PyTorch SDPA, with hardware counters explaining the throughput ranking. 60 data points, 3 figures.

item.title: Why Outer-Product Beats Vendor Sparse Libraries by up to 198x for LLM Attention Sparsity
item.description: Benchmarking dense dataflow strategies and sparse SpMSpM algorithms on NVIDIA T4 and AMD MI300x — 222 data points, 7 figures.
